summary:
Mission Architect is a browser-based simulator where players design and launch a real-style NASA space telescope mission, from first idea to orbit.

What it is: Players choose science objectives (one to three, across three levels), then select wavelengths, instruments and optics, an orbit, a launch vehicle, and a budget across the four mission segments: launch, space, ground and user. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it, then flies to its orbit with live telemetry. A final report scores the design and compares it to real missions such as Hubble, Webb, Chandra and Fermi.

How it addresses the challenge: It makes a whole space mission understandable through interactive 3D visualisation. It covers the mission concept, trajectory, timeline and spacecraft layout. Its steps follow NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies, with GMAT-style orbit readouts and a Mission Viz-style flight.

Why it matters: Mission design involves trade-offs between science goals, engineering limits and cost. Players learn that every choice affects the others, and that a mission succeeds only if all four segments work together. It needs no special software and runs on phones and computers.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Architect is a browser game that teaches how a space mission is designed. The player picks one to three science objectives across three levels, such as exoplanet atmospheres, black holes or the first galaxies. They then follow six steps modelled on NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies:

  1. Choose the science objectives.
  2. Choose wavelengths. Options that don't fit the objectives are disabled.
  3. Choose instruments and optics. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it.
  4. Compare four orbits, with a GMAT-style readout of period, signal delay and launcher performance.
  5. Pick a launch vehicle that can carry the spacecraft's mass to that orbit.
  6. Split a budget across the space, ground and user segments.

The game then runs a countdown and flies the spacecraft in 3D with live telemetry. It ends with a score out of 100 and an explanation of each choice. The report also compares the design to real missions (Hubble, Webb, Chandra, Fermi, Swift, TESS) and shows a mission timeline. Underfunding any of the four segments (launch, space, ground, user) makes the mission fail.

Benefits and intended impact

Players learn that mission design is a series of trade-offs, and that a mission needs all four segments to work. It runs in a browser on phones and computers, with no installation. It is meant for students and beginners, and it points them to the NASA resources it draws on.

Tools

I built it as a single HTML file in JavaScript and CSS, using Three.js for the 3D view and the Web Audio API for sound effects. The deck was made with Claude's Slides tool. I checked the game logic with Node scripts and captured the interface screenshots with Playwright. I did not use any special hardware.

Creativity

Instead of a quiz, the game lets players build a spacecraft and watch it fly. Every NASA resource in the challenge became a game mechanic, such as the CML progress bar and the GMAT-style orbit readout. Choices have realistic consequences: infrared telescopes do best at L2, X-ray telescopes do best in a highly elliptical orbit, and a rocket that is too small fails at launch.

Factors considered

Accuracy vs. simplicity: The numbers are simplified, inspired by real missions, and the game says so.

Accessibility: It works on phones, laptops and ipads it doesnt need to install.

Clear feedback: The game gives a reason for every score and failure.

Scope: It covers space telescopes only, not other mission types.
